blocks.en: Hello, young explorers, and welcome back to Michael's Morning Listening!
This is our twenty-first show together!
Today we visit a garden floating high above Earth, and an animal that wears a garden on its back.
One grows dinner in space.
One grows a forest in its fur.
Let's go!
High above Earth, inside the International Space Station, astronauts decided to grow salad.
But space has no soil, and no up or down.
So NASA built a small garden box called Veggie.
The seeds slept in little bags called plant pillows, under lamps of red and blue light.
Water moved along small wicks, because in space water does not fall — it floats.
Light, water and air are the primary needs of every plant, in space or on Earth.
After about a month, the crew picked red romaine lettuce, a variety called "Outredgeous." They cleaned each leaf with a wipe, then tasted it.
"It tastes like arugula," one astronaut said, to everyone's delight.
Cheers erupted around the table.
It takes courage to taste food grown where no food has ever grown.
Half the leaves were saved and frozen for study back on Earth.
The rest was eaten with olive oil and vinegar — the first space salad, grown high above the dinner table.
Now meet the three-toed sloth, the slowest mammal in the world.
It sleeps, eats leaves and barely moves — but look at its shaggy fur.
Each hair has tiny grooves that hold rainwater.
In that wet fur, green algae grows, turning the sloth's coat into a green garment.
The green is perfect camouflage: among the leaves, the sloth almost disappears.
But the garden has more tenants: tiny sloth moths live in the fur.
Once a week, the sloth climbs slowly down to the forest floor — a long and risky trip — and the moths lay their eggs in its droppings.
When the young moths grow up, they fly back into the fur.
When old moths die there, their bodies break down and feed the algae, like fertilizer.
It is no coincidence that sloths with more moths grow more algae.
And here is the astonishing part: scientists think the sloth sometimes licks its own fur and eats the algae for extra food.
In the dry season, when rain is rare, the green fades a little — but the garden waits for the next rain.
A sloth is not just one animal — it is a whole small world.
Here's today's idiom: "head in the clouds." Your head is where you think, and clouds are high in the sky, far away.
So if your head is in the clouds, your thoughts are far away — you are daydreaming, not paying attention.
Listen to this: During science class, Mia had her head in the clouds, dreaming about growing lettuce in space.
The teacher asked, "Mia, what do plants need?" Mia blinked and said, "Light, water, and...
a rocket?" The whole class laughed.
Mia's head had been in the clouds — but her dream was a good one!
Let's think about our stories.
Astronauts grew salad in space, and a sloth carries a garden in its fur.
Two questions for you.
First: if you could grow one food in space, what would it be, and why?
Second: the sloth's fur garden helps it hide and find food.
If you could wear a garden, what would you grow in it?
Talk about it with your family!
That's all for today, young explorers.
Remember: keep your feet on the ground, but let your dreams reach the stars.
Stay curious, and keep exploring.
See you tomorrow morning!
